Kling 4.0 brings a superpower: the ability to direct your scene frame by frame, with up to 10 keyframes in a single video.

This opens up a lot of possibilities. Here are a few cases, and at the end a simulation of a real spot.

How keyframes work

You load a start frame, up to 8 middle frames and an end frame, in order. Each keyframe is a moment the video must reach: Kling generates the motion between one frame and the next, and lands on each image as you gave it.
• The keyframes decide where the video goes: locations, framing, the state of the subject at each step.
• The prompt decides how it gets there: the type of transition, the camera move, the actions between frames, the sound.
• No prompt: @Kling_ai  chooses the transitions on its own.

Same keyframes, different prompt, completely different video. That is what the cases below show.

The keyframes (Cases 1, 2 and 3)
Five keyframes with the can standing in the center, same position and same size in every frame. Only the location changes:
1. Start: white studio
2. Middle: snow
3. Middle: sand
4. Middle: concert
5. End: rooftop at night

Key: when you edit the middle keyframes, lock the can's position and size but let light, shadow and the contact with the ground adapt to each place. With everything forced to stay pixel-identical, the sand and snow looked fake.

Case 3 — A hand carries the product into the next scene

A physical action becomes the transition.

Prompt
Between each keyframe, a hand enters the frame, picks up the can, and the camera follows it in one continuous movement into the next location, where the hand sets the can down in the center of the frame, in the same position and size, label facing the camera, and leaves the frame. The can is always the same can.

What happens: at every change a hand enters, picks up the can, carries it with a fast blurred movement into the next location and sets it down exactly where the keyframe has it. The label stays stable in the hand and through the motion blur.

Key: describe where the hand puts the product down ("center of the frame, same position and size"). That is what makes the action land on the keyframe.

A storm surge detonates against a concrete sea wall and the entire structure shudders through to its foundation.
Shot 1 — 0.0s to 5.0s — WS, low angle looking up from the waterline, crane mount. At 0.0s the frame is already wet: a brutalist concrete tidal barrier runs from frame left toward a vanishing point right, its vertical buttress fins stained dark by decades of salt, and a single sodium floodlight on a rusted mast burns orange against a bruised graphite sky. A swell arrives from behind camera and the first fraction of it — a wall of grey-green water, no crest, freight-train mass — climbs the parapet at 0.6s and detonates over it at 1.4s into a sheet of white spray that crosses the whole frame. The crane lifts with the impact at 1.2 m/s, rising from just above the waterline toward eye height on the parapet. Spray hangs airborne after the surge retreats, thinning slowly across the floodlight beam.
Hard cut.
Shot 2 — 5.0s to 10.5s — MCU, low, locked-off at the parapet. The last of the water drains back through the expansion joints in vertical ropes, and the retreat drags debris on gravity rather than wind: a length of splintered timber, a burst orange buoy, a scatter of stone aggregate, each tumbling with rotation and settling where physics puts it against the buttress fins. Residual water sheets off the concrete in one continuous film, then breaks into drips. Two gulls cross frame right to left, small and unhurried, and are gone.
Hard cut.
Shot 3 — 10.5s to 15.0s — EWS, high angle looking down from behind and above the barrier, slow dolly forward at 0.3 m/s. The ocean beyond is still working — long ground swell lines stacked to the horizon under the bruised sky — while the barrier itself has gone motionless and the suspended spray from the impact turns slowly in the floodlight beam. Nothing settles twice; the scene arrives at stillness with the water still moving behind it.
Camera law: 24mm anamorphic; movement family is crane rise at 1.2 m/s through shot one, locked-off through shot two, slow dolly forward at 0.3 m/s through shot three; the camera stays low for shots one and two and lifts above the parapet line only for shot three; 180 degree motion blur. Anti-default: droplets on the lens glass in the near foreground of shot two, defocused, never wiped.
Grade and audio: storm-desat palette — graphite, sodium-orange, cold grey-green — contrast pushed high with blacks crushed. Key light is the single sodium floodlight on the rusted mast, halation blooming where it burns through suspended spray. A gale ambient bed under five diegetic events — deep water impact on concrete, spray hiss across stone, water draining through expansion joints, timber cracking against the barrier, a distant fog signal.

Kling 4.0 shipped at 1080p for roughly 1 credit per second on @higgsfield for promotion time

i ran three tests on it 

Identical settings on all three, so the prompt is the only variable: 15s each, 1080p, text-to-video, no reference images.

Results:

Test 1 — environmental physics Storm surge detonating on a concrete sea wall. 15s, 3 shots.

Question: does heavy water carry real mass, or dissolve into particles?

It carried it. Gravity-bound drainage, no morphing, and debris that landed stayed landed across the cut.

Test 2 — camera discipline A gantry crane lowering a container. 15s, one unbroken take.

Question: does it hold a single take, or hide a cut when the move gets hard?

Zero cuts in 15 seconds. The load swung with real momentum.

It did ignore the dolly-zoom and push in physically instead.

Test 3 — macro physics, vertical One droplet into a still pool. 15s, 2 shots, 9:16.

Question: how far down the scale does the physics hold?

Rebound column, secondary droplet, real surface tension. Excellent in vertical.

Two misses: never fully settled; a stray droplet spawned at 0:03.

Three findings that held across all three:

Cuts landed early every time. i asked 5s / 10.5s / 8s, got roughly 4s / 10s / 6s. It compresses your timing.

Audio generated by the model

Dolly-zoom is the one move it refused.

Where it's strong: unbroken takes, heavy water and mechanical physics, object continuity across a cut.

Where it slips: precise cut timing, macro settling, compound camera moves.

Next: reference-to-video with elements, and editing an existing clip.

Prompts for all three tests below.
